stem: After discovering load balancers, suggested service candidates appear on the Service Mapping Home page under which tile?
rationale: Candidates Service Mapping wants you to turn into real maps queue under the Map tile. From there you review each suggestion (often derived from a load balancer's pool) and kick off mapping for the ones you want.

distractor_notes.A: The Fix tile surfaces maps with problems to remediate, not new candidates.
distractor_notes.B: Completed shows finished maps, not pending candidates.
distractor_notes.C: There isn't an 'Approve' tile in this flow for candidates.

stem: To begin configuring tag-based services, tag values must be defined where?
rationale: Tag-based mapping starts by defining the tag values inside tag categories. Those categorized values are what Service Mapping matches against to group resources into services — so the categories are the foundation you build first.

distractor_notes.A: 'Tag libraries' isn't the defining location for tag values in this flow.
distractor_notes.B: 'Tag catalogs' isn't the construct used to hold tag values here.
distractor_notes.C: Service families are a downstream grouping, not where raw tag values are defined.

stem: Tag-based mapping is best suited to which kind of environment?

options.text: Cloud or dynamic environments where resources are frequently created, renamed, or scaled
A single, small, rarely changing application
Environments with no metadata or tags at all
A static set of mainframe CIs

rationale: Tags shine when membership is fluid: in cloud/dynamic estates resources come and go and get renamed, so associating them by tag (rather than fixed topology) keeps the map current automatically as the fleet changes.

distractor_notes.B: A tiny stable service is better served by Manual Services — tags add needless dynamism.
distractor_notes.C: Tag-based mapping needs tags; with none it has nothing to match on.
distractor_notes.D: Static, unchanging CIs don't benefit from tag-driven flexibility.

stem: Which Service Mapping technique groups CIs at runtime via filter conditions or CMDB queries, with quick list/query visualization?
rationale: A Dynamic CI Group defines membership by a query/filter, so the group recomputes as data changes and you can view it instantly through list filters or saved CMDB queries. It's the lightweight, query-driven grouping option.

distractor_notes.A: Manual Services are hand-defined, not query-driven groupings.
distractor_notes.C: Top-down mapping builds a discovered service-to-CI hierarchy via patterns, not a CMDB query group.
distractor_notes.D: Tag-based mapping relies on tag maintenance, not arbitrary CMDB query filters.

stem: Which technique is most appropriate for a small application service that rarely changes and needs high availability?
rationale: A small, stable service benefits from a fixed, explicit definition. Manual Services let you hand-define the components once; because they don't depend on continual rediscovery or tag upkeep, the mapping stays reliable and immune to discovery hiccups.

distractor_notes.B: Dynamic CI groups suit evolving populations, not an immutable small service.
distractor_notes.C: Tag-based adds dynamism that a stable service doesn't need and must be maintained.
distractor_notes.D: Top-down's topological discovery is overkill for a single small, unchanging service.

stem: Which Service Mapping technique uses patterns to identify configuration details and establish process-to-process connections?
rationale: Top-down mapping is the pattern-driven approach: starting from an entry point, patterns identify each CI and discover the process-to-process connections that build the dependency tree. It's the core engine behind a true, automatically maintained service map.

distractor_notes.A: Tag-based classifies via tags; it doesn't parse patterns to find process links.
distractor_notes.B: Dynamic CI groups use membership queries, not pattern process discovery.
distractor_notes.D: Manual services are hand-built with no pattern-based discovery.

stem: Service Mapping gives operators visibility in Agent Workspace without leaving the workspace. Which two CI-associated items does this include?
rationale: Inside Agent Workspace, the service context surfaces operational signals on each CI — open incidents and active alerts (from Event Management/monitoring). That lets an operator triage impact without hopping to other modules.

distractor_notes.B: Software releases aren't the operational signals surfaced in this view.
distractor_notes.D: Problem KB articles aren't what the CI service context exposes here.

stem: From the Dependency View map, which button shows the related services for a configuration item?
rationale: The Group control reorganizes the Dependency View to surface the services a CI participates in, aggregating related items so you can see which services depend on it. The other buttons change layout or show attributes without revealing related services.

distractor_notes.A: Details opens the attribute pane for the selected CI.
distractor_notes.C: Force applies a layout algorithm; it doesn't group related services.
distractor_notes.D: Vertical just reorients the layout; it doesn't expose related services.

stem: Which best represents the breadth of CIs that running Service Mapping discovers?

options.text: Cloud Services, Applications, and CI Relationships
Hardware, Installed Software, and Network Gear only

rationale: Service Mapping is top-down and dependency-focused: it discovers the applications and cloud services that compose a business service and — critically — the relationships between them. Those relationships are its key differentiator versus pure inventory discovery.

distractor_notes.A: Licenses and bare IPs aren't the focus of service-level mapping.
distractor_notes.C: Licenses aren't a Service Mapping output; applications and cloud services are.
distractor_notes.D: That's an inventory/horizontal-discovery framing; Service Mapping centers on services and relationships.

stem: On the Service Mapping Home page, which tile lists maps that have discovery problems needing remediation?
rationale: The Fix tile collects maps with issues — credential errors, broken connections, generic apps — so an operator can work the remediation queue. Map holds candidates to discover; Completed holds healthy finished maps.

distractor_notes.A: Map is for new/candidate services to discover, not problems.
distractor_notes.C: Schedule isn't a status tile for remediation.
distractor_notes.D: Completed shows successfully mapped services.

stem: A key advantage of using a Dynamic CI Group over a fully mapped service is what?

options.text: It doesn't require a Service Mapping license and visualizes via list filters/CMDB queries
It guarantees a complete top-down dependency tree
It eliminates the need for the CMDB

rationale: Dynamic CI Groups are a CMDB query construct — no Service Mapping license needed — and you visualize them instantly through list filters or saved queries. The trade-off is they don't perform pattern-based dependency discovery.

distractor_notes.B: Dynamic groups don't produce a discovered dependency tree.
distractor_notes.C: Process-to-process discovery is top-down mapping's job, not a dynamic group's.
distractor_notes.D: They live in the CMDB; they don't replace it.

stem: Which is a defining trait of a Manual Service compared with top-down mapping?

options.text: Its components are defined explicitly by an administrator rather than discovered by patterns
It is rediscovered automatically on every schedule
It requires tag categories to function
It builds connections using process classifiers

rationale: Manual Services are hand-authored: the admin specifies the CIs and relationships directly. There's no pattern discovery involved, which is why they're best for small, stable services where a fixed definition is more reliable than continual rediscovery.

distractor_notes.B: Manual services aren't pattern-rediscovered; they're maintained by hand.
distractor_notes.C: Tag categories belong to tag-based mapping, not manual services.
distractor_notes.D: Process classifiers drive pattern-based discovery, not manual definitions.

stem: After Service Mapping suggests service candidates from discovered load balancers, what is the intended next administrator action?

options.text: Review each candidate, adjust as needed, and initiate mapping for the ones to keep

rationale: Candidates are suggestions, not finished maps. The admin reviews them on the Map tile, tweaks names/scope, and starts mapping for the real services — turning the load balancer's pools into proper, maintained service maps.

distractor_notes.A: Disabling the LB would harm production, not map services.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting them throws away useful suggestions.
distractor_notes.D: Candidates aren't incidents; they're proposed services.

stem: Why does an automatically discovered (top-down) service map require less ongoing maintenance than a manually built one?

options.text: Because it ignores new CIs entirely
Scheduled rediscovery updates the map automatically as the environment changes
Because it never changes once created

rationale: Pattern-discovered maps refresh themselves on a schedule, so adds, removals, and version changes flow into the map without hand-editing. A manual map has to be updated by a person every time the environment shifts.

distractor_notes.A: It does store relationships; that's the whole point of the map.
distractor_notes.B: Rediscovery picks up new CIs rather than ignoring them.
distractor_notes.D: Environments change constantly — that's exactly why automatic rediscovery helps.

stem: What role does Predictive Intelligence play in ML-powered Service Mapping?

options.text: It monitors the performance of scheduled jobs
It generates connection suggestions and confidence scores from processed discovery data
It displays the readiness status of prerequisites
It activates and manages discovery probes

rationale: Predictive Intelligence analyzes discovery data to propose likely connections and assign a confidence score to each, so administrators can quickly accept or dismiss suggested dependencies. It augments mapping with ML, rather than running probes or dashboards.

distractor_notes.A: Job performance monitoring is a Performance Analytics concern.
distractor_notes.C: Readiness status is shown on dashboards; PI informs suggestions, not status display.
distractor_notes.D: Probe management belongs to the Discovery engine.

stem: On the Application Service Readiness dashboard, what does the confidence level represent?

options.text: The readiness state of all prerequisites
The probability that a discovered connection belongs to the application service
The probability that a given server hosts the application
The frequency of scheduled jobs for a connection

rationale: Confidence quantifies how sure the engine is that an observed connection truly belongs to the service — derived from signal count, protocol validation, and topology consistency. Higher confidence means the mapping is more likely correct and can be trusted with less manual review.

distractor_notes.A: Prerequisite readiness is shown separately as a state, not as confidence.
distractor_notes.C: Confidence is about connection membership in the service, not host-hosting probability.
distractor_notes.D: Job frequency is unrelated to mapping confidence.

stem: What does the Top 10 Service Issues report show in ML-powered Service Mapping?

options.text: The application services most affected by ML-related mapping issues
The training percentage of application fingerprints
A summary of all active scheduled jobs
The readiness status of all application services

rationale: The report ranks the services experiencing the biggest impact from ML-detected mapping issues, so operators can prioritize the most critical remediation first. Fingerprint training and job summaries live in other views.

distractor_notes.B: Fingerprint training status is shown in fingerprint-specific views.
distractor_notes.C: Scheduled-job summaries are on the jobs dashboard.
distractor_notes.D: Holistic readiness status is a different dashboard view.

stem: How does a confidence score from Predictive Intelligence help an administrator?

options.text: It indicates how much to trust a suggested connection
It schedules the next discovery run

rationale: A confidence score lets you triage suggestions: high-confidence connections can be auto-accepted, while lower-confidence ones get human review. It turns ML output into actionable, risk-graded decisions rather than blind automation.

distractor_notes.B: Credential assignment is separate from confidence scoring.
distractor_notes.C: Reconciliation precedence is a CMDB setting, unrelated to PI confidence.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduling is handled by discovery schedules, not confidence scores.

stem: How does ML-powered Service Mapping use observed network traffic?

options.text: It blocks traffic that doesn't match a pattern
It reroutes production traffic through the MID Server
It analyzes traffic (e.g., NetFlow/netstat) to infer likely connections and suggest dependencies
It replaces credentials with traffic capture

rationale: Traffic-based connection discovery studies flow data to see who actually talks to whom, surfacing candidate connections that pure pattern discovery might miss. The ML layer then scores and suggests those dependencies for confirmation.

distractor_notes.A: Service Mapping observes traffic; it doesn't block it.
distractor_notes.B: It doesn't reroute production traffic.
distractor_notes.D: Traffic analysis complements, but doesn't replace, credentialed discovery.

stem: In ML-powered Service Mapping, what is an application fingerprint used for?

options.text: Characterizing an application so its connections and relationships can be evaluated/learned

rationale: Fingerprints capture an application's identifying characteristics so the ML engine can recognize it and evaluate its likely relationships with other CIs. They feed the learning/scoring that produces connection suggestions.

distractor_notes.A: Encryption is handled by TLS, not fingerprints.
distractor_notes.B: Fingerprints support ML evaluation; they don't replace IRE identifiers.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduling is a discovery-schedule function.

stem: Besides confidence, what else does the Application Service Readiness dashboard surface?

options.text: The list of open incidents company-wide
The readiness state of prerequisites needed for accurate mapping

rationale: The dashboard shows whether the prerequisites for reliable mapping are in place (readiness state) alongside confidence figures, helping teams see what still needs attention before trusting a map. Incident lists and MID schedules live elsewhere.

distractor_notes.A: MID Server upgrade scheduling is a MID Server concern.
distractor_notes.B: Reconciliation precedence is a CMDB I&R configuration.
distractor_notes.C: Company-wide incident lists aren't this dashboard's purpose.

stem: Which task is NOT a function of Predictive Intelligence in Service Mapping?

options.text: Helping prioritize which mappings to trust automatically
Executing discovery probes against target hosts
Assigning a confidence score to suggested connections

rationale: Running probes against hosts is the Discovery engine/MID Server's job. Predictive Intelligence works on already-collected data — proposing connections, scoring confidence, and helping triage what to trust. It analyzes; it doesn't probe.

distractor_notes.A: Prioritizing trust based on confidence is a PI benefit.
distractor_notes.B: Suggesting connections is a core PI function.
distractor_notes.D: Confidence scoring is exactly what PI provides.

stem: Traditional discovery leaves gaps where some connections between tiers aren't found. Which capability proposes likely missing connections by learning from existing maps?
rationale: ML-powered Service Mapping uses Predictive Intelligence to suggest connections that discovery missed, based on patterns learned from existing maps — helping close gaps that pattern and traffic methods didn't catch.

distractor_notes.B: Reconciliation rules govern attribute authority, not connection prediction.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: UI policies change form behavior.

stem: ML proposes several possible missing connections for a service. What is the appropriate way to handle these before they affect the map?

options.text: Review and accept/reject the suggested connections
Automatically trust every suggestion without review

rationale: ML connection suggestions are presented for human review — you accept the correct ones and reject the rest — so the map improves without blindly trusting predictions.

distractor_notes.B: Blindly accepting predictions can introduce wrong connections.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting the service discards the map.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling the MID Server stops discovery.

stem: For ML connection suggestions to be useful, what does the model rely on to learn what 'normal' connections look like?

options.text: Patterns learned from existing, successfully mapped services

rationale: Predictive Intelligence for Service Mapping learns from existing maps to recognize likely connections, so a healthy base of well-mapped services improves the quality of its suggestions.

distractor_notes.B: Branding is cosmetic and irrelevant to ML training.
distractor_notes.C: Catalog categories organize catalog items, not map learning.
distractor_notes.D: Email templates are unrelated to ML.

stem: A team wants to prioritize remediation by seeing which services have the most mapping problems. Which ML-driven report helps focus that effort?
rationale: The Top 10 Service Issues report surfaces the services with the most issues, letting teams prioritize the highest-impact remediation first.

distractor_notes.B: CMDB Health completeness is broader CMDB quality, not the ML service-issue ranking.
distractor_notes.C: Branding jobs are cosmetic.
distractor_notes.D: The ECC Queue shows MID Server messages, not a service-issue ranking.

stem: A customer wants the advanced ML connection-suggestion capabilities for Service Mapping. What should they confirm they have?

options.text: A larger MID Server heap only

rationale: Advanced ML-powered capabilities are part of the Service Mapping Plus entitlement, so customers should confirm they have the right edition to use them.

distractor_notes.B: MID Server sizing helps performance but doesn't unlock ML features.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists are unrelated.
distractor_notes.D: Coalesce matches import records.

stem: After accepting valid ML connection suggestions over time, what outcome should a team expect?

options.text: More complete service maps with fewer manual interventions

rationale: Accepting good ML suggestions fills gaps that discovery missed, yielding more complete maps and reducing the manual work of hunting down connections.

distractor_notes.B: ML suggestions don't encrypt the CMDB.
distractor_notes.C: Discovery still needs credentials to access targets.
distractor_notes.D: Patterns remain; ML complements them.

stem: How should ML-powered suggestions be positioned relative to pattern-based discovery?

options.text: As a complement that fills gaps, not a replacement for patterns
As a full replacement for all patterns
As a way to avoid having any credentials

rationale: ML augments pattern-based discovery by suggesting connections it missed; patterns still do the primary, deterministic mapping. They work together.

distractor_notes.B: ML doesn't replace deterministic patterns.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials are still required for discovery.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation is a separate CMDB concept.

stem: A newly deployed instance with very few existing service maps gets low-quality ML suggestions. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: There isn't enough mapped data yet for the model to learn from
The instance time zone is wrong
There are too many watch lists

rationale: ML quality depends on learning from existing maps; with few maps, the model has little to learn from, so suggestions improve as more services are mapped successfully.

distractor_notes.B: Time zone affects scheduling/display, not ML quality.
distractor_notes.C: Branding is cosmetic.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists are unrelated to ML training.

stem: What is the primary goal of ML-powered Service Mapping?

options.text: Improve map completeness by predicting connections discovery missed

rationale: Its goal is more complete maps via predicted connections, reducing blind spots left by purely deterministic discovery.

distractor_notes.B: It enriches the CMDB, not replaces it.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't encrypt maps.
distractor_notes.D: SLA notifications are service-level management.

stem: What does the Top 10 Service Issues report primarily help teams do?

options.text: Prioritize remediation on the services with the most issues

rationale: It ranks services by issue volume so teams fix the highest-impact problems first.

distractor_notes.B: Hardware ordering is a catalog/asset task.
distractor_notes.C: SSO is authentication configuration.
distractor_notes.D: Email properties are unrelated.

stem: Which TWO are true about ML-powered Service Mapping?

options.text: It suggests connections that discovery may have missed
Suggestions are reviewed before being applied
It removes the need for credentials

rationale: ML proposes missed connections and those suggestions are reviewed before acceptance. It doesn't remove credential requirements or replace the CMDB.

distractor_notes.C: Discovery still needs credentials.
distractor_notes.D: The CMDB remains the system of record.

stem: Which TWO factors improve ML suggestion quality in Service Mapping?

options.text: A larger base of successfully mapped services to learn from
Reviewing and accepting only correct suggestions over time

rationale: More good maps give the model more to learn from, and careful review reinforces correct outcomes. Turning off Discovery or deleting maps reduces the data ML depends on.

distractor_notes.C: Discovery provides the deterministic base maps ML builds on.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting maps removes the learning data.
